chunks.text: In short
Seven pages do almost all the work: home, menu, hours-and-location, reservations, story, contact, and one current promotion.
Pages you probably do not need: separate "events" page, blog, gallery (the site itself is the gallery).
Structure that earns its keep: every page answers a hungry-at-11 PM question in under 3 taps.
Leer este artículo en español →
Why seven?

Picture the guest who decides whether to eat at your place tonight. She is on the sidewalk a block away, phone in one hand, deciding between you and the spot with the line out front. She thumbs your name, the site loads, and in a few seconds she is either walking toward your door or tapping back to the map. What should be on a restaurant website is whatever answers her three questions before she gives up: what kind of food, where, and how to book. Seven pages carry that load. Everything else is weight.

This is a field guide, not a theory of websites. Each of the seven pages below has one job, and the test for every page is the same: does it move a real person from the sidewalk to a booked table, or does it just sit there. A "Careers" page nobody updates, an "Awards" list from three years ago, a "Gallery" of forty captionless photos, each one dilutes the pages that convert and muddies what Google thinks the site is about. If a page does not have a job, it does not earn its place on the nav bar.

The diner’s walk from search result to front door, as five stations, each carried by one of the seven pages. Station one, the five-second test: the homepage answers what kind of food, where, and how to book before the thumb moves on, fail it and the visit ends on the sidewalk. Station two, the decision: the menu page, in real H T M L text, lets the diner pick what to eat before they arrive, a P D F here means pinch-and-zoom in direct sunlight. Station three, the tiebreak: the about page gives a first-time customer a reason to choose you over the identical-looking restaurant next door, specifics, not passion-for-food copy. Station four, the conversion: the reservations or order page turns intent into action in the fewest possible taps, with the widget embedded rather than linked out. Station five, the arrival: location and hours remove every friction point between I want to go and I am walking in the door. Two of the seven pages sit off the walk on purpose: private events catches the high-value inquiry that has no Google Business Profile field, and contact catches everyone who needs a human without calling during dinner rush.
1. Homepage.
Job: answer three questions in under five seconds, what kind of food, where, and how to book.

Your homepage is not your autobiography. It is a decision tool. A first-time visitor is standing on the sidewalk, phone in hand, deciding between you and the place next door. They need: cuisine type, neighborhood, vibe, hours, and a reservation button. Everything else is below the fold.
One-sentence pitch under your name (e.g., "Neighborhood Italian · Silver Spring · family-run since 1998")
Today's hours , visible without scrolling
Reservation or order-online button, visible without scrolling
One hero photo that shows the room or the food, not a stock image, not a logo on black
A short social proof signal: a review quote, a press mention, a star rating
2. Menu.
Job: let someone decide what to eat before they arrive.

On nearly every restaurant site, this is the most-visited page, and the one most restaurants get wrong. The menu should be real H T M L text, not a P D F, not a photo of a printed card, not an iframe from a third-party widget. Real text means: Google can crawl it, phones can render it at readable sizes, screen readers can read it, and you can update it in thirty seconds when you change the prix fixe.
Dish names, descriptions, and prices in real text
Organized by course or category with clear headings
Dietary markers (V, VG, GF) if you have them
A "last updated" date so customers know the prices are current
If your menu is a P D F, you have already lost the customer who is reading it on a phone in direct sunlight.

Two versions of the same menu, side by side. The first, marked as what is there now, is a P D F link, diners pinch and zoom on a phone, Google cannot crawl the dish names, screen readers cannot read it, and updating the prix fixe means re-exporting and re-uploading the file. The second, marked as what should be there, is real H T M L, dish names, descriptions, and prices in plain text, organized by course with dietary markers and a last-updated date. Google indexes every dish, the page renders at readable sizes on every phone, screen readers can read it, and a price change takes thirty seconds.
3. About / Our Story.
Job: give a first-time customer a reason to choose you over the identical-looking restaurant next door.

This page is where you differentiate. Not with a wall of text about your "passion for food", every restaurant says that. With specifics: where you source, who cooks, how long you have been here, what the room looks like, why this neighborhood. Two paragraphs and a real photo of the team is worth more than a thousand words of generic "our philosophy" copy.
4. Reservations / Order Online.
Job: convert intent into action with the fewest possible clicks.

This might be a dedicated page or a persistent button that lives on every page, either way, the customer should never be more than one tap away from booking a table or starting an order. If you use OpenTable, Resy, Tock, or another platform, embed the widget directly in your page rather than linking out. Every click away from your site is a chance for the customer to get distracted.

If you do your own takeout or delivery, route orders through your P O S (Toast, Square, ChowNow) rather than through third-party marketplace apps. The commission a marketplace keeps, often 15, 30% per order, stays in the house on every order that comes through your own page instead.
From the floor

The test I run on this page is a stopwatch. From a cold homepage on my phone, how many taps to a held table? If it is more than two, something is in the way, a splash screen, a "reservations" link that opens a new tab, a widget that takes a beat to load on the dining-room Wi-Fi. I would rather the booking button be the loudest thing above the fold and the prettiest hero photo come second. Nobody ever left because the reserve button was too easy to find.
5. Private Events / Catering.
Job: capture high-value inquiries that have nowhere to live on Google.

This is the page most restaurants forget, and it is often the highest-revenue page on the site. Private events, buyouts, catering menus, and group bookings do not have a Google Business Profile field. If someone searches "private dining Bethesda" and you do not have a page with those words on it, you are invisible to that search entirely.
What spaces you offer (private room, patio buyout, full restaurant)
Capacity ranges
A sample catering or events menu (even a simplified one)
A simple inquiry form: name, email, date, party size, and a "tell us more" field
6. Location & Hours.
Job: remove every possible friction point between "I want to go" and "I am walking in the door."

This page should have: your full address as copyable text (not an image), an embedded Google Map, today's hours prominently displayed, parking information, public transit directions if applicable, and your phone number as a tap-to-call link. If you have multiple locations, each one gets its own section with its own map and hours.
7. Contact.
Job: give people a way to reach a human without calling during dinner rush.

A working contact form , your email, your phone, and your social links. Keep it simple. The form should ask for name, email, and message, nothing else. If you want to capture different types of inquiries (press, events, general), a single dropdown is fine. Do not make people fill out a twelve-field form to ask when you open on Sundays.
Pages you probably do not need.
Cut these unless you have a specific, active reason to keep them:
Gallery. Put your best three photos on the homepage and your menu. A dedicated gallery page with forty unlabeled images is a bounce factory.

Blog. Unless you are going to publish at least once a month with real content, an empty blog page with one post from two years ago hurts more than it helps. It tells Google and customers that the site is neglected.
Awards / Press. Fold a short press mention into the homepage or About page. A full page dedicated to awards reads as self-congratulatory unless you are updating it regularly.
Careers. Use your Google Business Profile or a jobs platform instead. A "Careers" page with no listings looks like you are either not hiring or not maintaining your site.

Four pages most independent restaurants should drop from the nav, each with the reason. Gallery, a page of forty unlabeled photos is a bounce factory; put the best three on the homepage and the menu instead. Blog, an empty blog with one post from two years ago tells Google and customers the site is neglected; only keep one if you will publish at least once a month. Awards or press, a full page reads as self-congratulatory unless updated; fold a short mention into the homepage or About. Careers, a page with no listings looks like you are not hiring or not maintaining the site; use the Google Business Profile or a jobs platform instead.
The structure that earns its keep.

A three-question decision tree for any page you are tempted to add to a restaurant site. Question one, does the page answer a question a first-time customer would actually type into Google before deciding to visit? Yes, keep it. The seven core pages all do. No, move to question two. Question two, does the page handle an inquiry that nothing else on the site captures, like private events or catering? Yes, keep it. The high-value inquiries need a dedicated landing or they leak to a generic contact form. No, move to question three. Question three, will you actually maintain this page on a monthly cadence? Yes, keep it. A blog with monthly posts, a press page with current mentions, a careers page with active listings all earn their place. No, cut it. An empty page hurts more than the absence; Google reads it as a neglected site, and customers read it the same way.

Build the page in this order. The sequence is not about importance, every one of the seven matters, it is about unblocking the diner's walk earliest. Ship the pages that get a hungry stranger from the search result to a held table first; ship the pages that catch the off-the-walk inquiries last. Each step maps to a slot in your sitemap .
Build the Menu page first, real H T M L, organized by course, priced, dated. It is the most-visited page; if nothing else ships, this one has to.
Build the Location & Hours page next, copyable address, embedded map, today's hours, parking, transit. This is the arrival; it removes the last friction before the door.
Wire up Reservations / Order, embed the widget, make it one tap, and put the button above the fold on every page.
Build the Homepage on top of those three, cuisine, location, vibe, today's hours, and the C T A , all answered in the first few seconds.
Write the About / Our Story page, sourcing, team, the room, one real photo. This is the tiebreak, so it can follow the conversion path, not lead it.
Stand up the Private Events page, spaces, capacity ranges, a sample menu, an inquiry form. It catches the high-value inquiry that has nowhere else to land.
Finish with Contact, a working form, email, phone, social. Keep it to name, email, and message.
Seven pages. Each one has a job. If your site has more than this, ask yourself what each extra page is doing. If the answer is "nothing," cut it. Your visitors and Google will both thank you.
Key takeaways
The home page exists to answer one question: "is this what I want tonight?"
The menu page must be H T M L, not a P D F, PDFs are dead in mobile + AI search.
Reservations belong above the fold on every page, not buried in a contact form.
Story page is the second most important after menu, it is what guests share to convince a friend.
Delete the "events" page; weave events into the home page as a current-promotion strip.
